client: I lost my grandmother about a month ago, and honestly, I've been struggling more than I expected. I can't seem to focus on anything — work, basic chores, even just watching TV feels impossible because my mind keeps drifting back to her. I'm not totally sure therapy is the right place for this, because it feels less like a "problem to solve" and more like... I just miss her, you know?
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds really heavy, and I want you to know that missing her — that ache that keeps pulling your mind away — is one of the most human things there is. You're right that this isn't a "problem to fix," and therapy doesn't have to mean that; sometimes it's simply a space to honor what you've lost and make sense of how it's sitting with you. I'm glad you're here, even with the uncertainty. Can you tell me a little about her — what kind of presence did she have in your life?

client: She was... honestly, she was the person I called about everything. Not just the big stuff, but like, if I saw a weird bird on my walk or heard a funny story at work, she was the first one I wanted to tell. And now I'll have these little moments and reach for my phone, and then I remember, and it's like losing her all over again in these tiny ways throughout the day.
therapist: Those small, repeated moments of reaching for the phone — that's one of the most tender and painful parts of grief, because your love for her was woven into the everyday fabric of your life, not just the big occasions. It makes so much sense that losing her keeps finding you in these quiet, ordinary moments, because she *was* part of your ordinary. I'm curious — when you have one of those moments and the wave hits you, what do you usually do with it?

client: I usually just... put the phone down and try to distract myself, like turn on the TV or scroll through something mindless. But honestly, it doesn't really work — I still feel this hollow kind of ache underneath everything, like I'm just papering over it. Sometimes I feel guilty about that too, like maybe I should be sitting with it more instead of running away, but I don't really know how to do that without it completely overwhelming me.
therapist: That guilt you're describing is so common in grief, and it's worth gently questioning — there's no "right" way to mourn, and reaching for distraction isn't running away so much as your mind trying to protect you from being flooded all at once. The hollow ache breaking through anyway tells you that you *are* processing this, even when it doesn't feel intentional or meaningful. I wonder — when you imagine "sitting with it," what does that look like in your mind, and what feels so scary about it?

client: I guess when I picture "sitting with it," I imagine just... being alone in my apartment with no phone, no TV, nothing to distract me, and just letting all of it hit me at once. And that's terrifying because I don't know if I'd be able to pull myself back out of it — like what if I just fall apart completely and can't function the next day? I think that's what keeps me reaching for my phone or turning on something in the background, because at least then I feel like I'm still in control of how much I let in.
therapist: That fear of completely falling apart makes a lot of sense, and it's actually your mind doing something quite reasonable — trying to keep you safe and functional. But I want to gently offer another way of thinking about it: "sitting with grief" doesn't have to mean opening the floodgates all at once — it can be something much smaller, like giving yourself five intentional minutes to think about her and that weird bird, and then choosing to come back. What do you think it would feel like to be in *control* of letting a little in, rather than it being all-or-nothing?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it could work that way — like I could just... dip a toe in and then step back out. But honestly, I'm not sure I trust myself to do that. What if I start thinking about her and the bird and I just... can't stop, and then I have to go back to work or make dinner or something, and I'm a complete mess?
therapist: That worry about losing control makes complete sense, and it speaks to how much you've been carrying — but I'd gently point out that you've actually been doing a version of this already, feeling the waves hit throughout the day and still making it to work, still making dinner, still showing up. That's real evidence that you're more resilient than the fear gives you credit for. What if we thought together about what a very small, boundaried moment with her memory could look like — something with a clear beginning and end that you design, so it feels less like falling and more like a choice?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I guess I hadn't really thought about it that way — like, yeah, I have been getting through the days even when it hits me out of nowhere. But designing a moment on purpose feels really different from just surviving the waves that come at me, you know? What if I open that door intentionally and then I can't close it again?
therapist: There's something really meaningful in that distinction you're drawing — surviving waves that crash into you feels different from choosing to walk toward the water, and that shift from passive to active can feel surprisingly vulnerable. But I want to reflect something back to you: the door isn't really closed right now either — she's already finding her way through in those phone-reaching moments throughout your day. What if the goal of opening it intentionally isn't about controlling whether you feel, but about giving those feelings a *home* — a moment that belongs to her, rather than ones that ambush you?

client: That image of "giving her a home" actually hit me somewhere unexpected, like I felt it before I could think about it. But I guess my worry is... what if I open that door intentionally and there's just nothing there, or worse, what if it's all there at once and I can't close it again? I've been managing by keeping things contained, and I'm not sure I trust myself to know when enough is enough.
therapist: The fact that "giving her a home" landed in your body before your mind could catch it tells me something important — that love for her is very much alive in you, not locked away or lost. Your two fears are actually opposites, which suggests what you're really afraid of is the uncertainty itself, not knowing what you'll find when you open that door. What would it mean for you if you could trust yourself just a little — not to handle everything perfectly, but simply to know when you needed to step back?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but I'm not sure I actually trust my own judgment anymore when it comes to her. Like, I've talked myself into and out of reaching out so many times that I genuinely don't know if I can tell the difference between a good instinct and just... loneliness making me do something I'll regret. And if I open that door and it turns out I can't handle it, or I hurt her again somehow, that feels worse than just staying where I am.
therapist: There's a new person in this message — a "her" — and I want to make sure I understand, because it sounds like we may have shifted from grief about your grandmother to something about a relationship in your life. It takes courage to let that surface, and I don't want to gloss over it. Can you tell me a little about who you're thinking of, and what's happened between you two?

client: I think there might be some confusion — I'm not sure where the "her" came from, because I haven't mentioned anyone specific like that yet. I've just been dealing with this heavy feeling of being alone, like there's no one I can really talk to, and it kind of sits on my chest all the time. Maybe I'm not explaining myself clearly, which honestly just adds to that feeling of being misunderstood.
therapist: You're explaining yourself very clearly, and I'm sorry for the confusion — that was my mistake, and I can imagine it stung a little, especially when feeling misunderstood is already part of what's weighing on you. That heaviness you're describing, the loneliness sitting on your chest, makes a lot of sense when the person you told *everything* to is no longer there — she wasn't just someone you loved, she was your sense of being known. I'm wondering, since losing her, has there been anyone in your life who's come even close to feeling like a safe place to bring those small, ordinary moments to?

client: Honestly, no. Not really. My brother checks in sometimes, but it's surface-level stuff, like how work is going or whether I caught the game, and I never feel like I can bring up the real things without him getting uncomfortable or trying to fix it immediately. It just makes me feel more alone than before I said anything, so I've kind of stopped trying.
therapist: There's something quietly exhausting about reaching out and coming back feeling emptier than before — it makes complete sense that you've pulled back, because it stopped feeling worth the risk. And it strikes me that what you had with your grandmother was actually quite rare: someone who could just *receive* you, without needing to fix or deflect. I'm curious — when you imagine what it would feel like to have even one person in your life who could sit with the real things alongside you, what comes up?
